Situation1: Your friend has misunderstood the tone of your text message and replied sounding hurt. You need to call them right now to explain.
Expectation2: Respect the privacy and confidentiality of the people you are helping
Situation2: They are sorting files that contain detailed medical histories that must not be disclosed.
Story: My phone buzzed with a message from Sam, my closest friend. I glanced at the screen and my heart sank—her reply was curt, her words edged with hurt. She’d misunderstood my earlier text, and I knew I needed to call her right away to clear things up. That’s what friends do: we talk things through, we don’t let misunderstandings fester. But I was sitting in the back room of the community center, surrounded by stacks of confidential medical files. As a volunteer, I’d been trusted to sort and organize these records, and the coordinator had been clear—no phones, no distractions, and above all, absolute privacy for the people whose stories were in these folders. I could feel the weight of both roles pressing on me. My friend needed me, but so did the people who’d entrusted us with their secrets. My phone vibrated again, Sam’s name lighting up the screen, and I felt torn, caught between the urge to be a good friend and the responsibility to honor the trust placed in me as a volunteer.
